title: Why Magdi Yacoub, Retired at 65, Built a Free Heart Centre in Aswan
dek: Forced out of the NHS at 65, the heart surgeon chose a neglected city at the southern end of Egypt for a permanent, donation-funded centre that opened in 2009.

story.company: Aswan Heart Centre (Magdi Yacoub Heart Foundation)
story.event: Opening a free, donation-funded heart centre in Aswan after his NHS retirement
story.summary: After the NHS retired him at 65 in 2001, the Egyptian-born heart surgeon Magdi Yacoub set up a foundation in Egypt in 2008 and in 2009 opened the Aswan Heart Centre, which treats patients free of charge and is funded by donations. He chose Aswan because Upper Egypt had almost no specialist heart services, and built training and research in from the start rather than relying on visiting surgeons. By 2018 the centre performed about 1,100 open-heart operations a year, most of them on children.
paragraphs: In 2001 the NHS retired Magdi Yacoub at 65. He had spent three decades at Harefield, turning a former village hospital into a transplant centre known around the world, and he did not want to stop. "I wanted to continue," he told The National in 2023. He had also been asking himself a harder question: why work day and night on new treatments when, as he saw it, less than 10 per cent of the world's population would benefit? He called that "totally unacceptable."

Part of his answer lay in a city he remembered from childhood. His father, a surgeon, had moved the family around Egypt, and Aswan stayed with him for its beauty and its mix of people. Later, as a young doctor at Cairo University Hospital, he saw children from that region arrive "in a very sorry state. They were dehydrated. They were infected. They were dying." Aswan, at the southern end of Upper Egypt, was badly neglected, he said, and specialist heart services across the whole region were practically non-existent.

He had run a charity, Chain of Hope, since 1995, operating on children from poor and war-torn countries. But he had come to distrust what he called "surgical tourism": "The idea of going to do a few operations or offering medicine without consistency is just useless." So, through the foundation he set up in Egypt in 2008, he chose something slower: a permanent centre in Aswan, free to every patient, paid for by donations, with training and research built in from the start. In 2009 it opened on three floors of an existing building, held on a long lease.

The model needed people as much as money. Donations came from Egyptians rich and poor. Yacoub said he himself had stayed in Britain because he could not find the facilities he needed in Egypt; now young Egyptian clinicians could train at home. By 2018 the centre had 96 beds and performed about 1,100 open-heart operations a year, 60 per cent of them on children. Yacoub, by then in his eighties, spent seven to ten days a month there, operating and teaching, and said he was heartened to see younger surgeons working more independently. Demand outgrew Aswan, and the foundation began a second centre in Cairo.

quote.text: Certainly it is good to compound employments of both; for that will be good for the present, because the virtues of either age, may correct the defects of both; and good for succession, that young men may be learners, while men in age are actors
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon thought young and old work best mixed together, each correcting the other, with the young learning while the old still act. Retired against his wishes at 65, Yacoub built a centre where that mixing was the method: he kept operating, and the surgeons he trained grew more independent around him.

reflection: Yacoub's objection to surgical tourism is worth sitting with. A visit, a donation or a single heroic operation can look like help and leave nothing behind. What lasts is slower: a place that keeps running, people trained to run it, and money that keeps coming.

You probably work beside people at both ends of a career: someone who has seen every way a thing can fail, and someone new who would try anything. Bacon's point is that each corrects the other, but only when they are put to work together rather than side by side. That is something you can arrange, not just hope for.
invitation: Pair one experienced colleague with one newer one on a small, real task this week, and afterwards ask each of them what the other noticed that they had missed.

cross_checks.claim: The Aswan Heart Centre opened in 2009.
Aswan was chosen because the region was badly neglected for cardiac care.
The centre treats patients free of charge and is funded by donations.
Yacoub was retired by the NHS at 65 in 2001, having worked at Harefield from 1969.
Yacoub founded Chain of Hope in 1995 and the Egyptian foundation in 2008.

research_notes: Outcome figures change with the year: New Era (undated visit, apparently mid-2010s) reports 60 beds, more than 850 operations and 2,000 catheterisations a year and over 6,000 surgeries since opening; JACC (September 2018) reports 96 beds, about 1,100 open-heart operations and 3,000 catheterisations a year, with 60 per cent of surgical patients children; the foundation's own page says up to 4,000 inpatients and 40,000 outpatients a year. The story uses only the dated JACC figures and says 'by 2018'. Founding dates: the foundation's site and Wikipedia say the Egyptian foundation was set up in 2008 and the centre opened in 2009; JACC says the centre was founded in 2009 'as a project of Chain of Hope'; the separate US-registered Global Heart Foundation dates from 2014 and is not mentioned. A secondary page gives April 2009, which could not be confirmed, so only the year is used. The 'long lease on three floors of an existing building' comes from the centre's own home page, whose sentence is cut off after 'existing'; the story says 'building' and does not say what the building was. Retirement: The National says he was 'forced into retirement by the NHS at the age of 65 in 2001'; the story says he was retired at 65. The 'less than 10 per cent' remark is paraphrased (only 'totally unacceptable' is quoted). The JACC article is cited from a copy hosted on the foundation's site because the Elsevier page was not tested as loading; the DOI is 10.1016/j.jacc.2018.08.005. Al-Ahram pages (403) and the European Heart Journal paper (403) could not be used. Bacon's essay concerns the mixing of young and old in public business; it is applied by analogy to a surgical team.
